before.quote: Let $K$ be a field and let $v$ be a discrete valuation on $K$ ([[def-discrete-valuation]]). Its **valuation ring** is $$ V_v:=\{x\in K:v(x)\ge 0\}. $$ This is a valuation ring in the sense of [[def-valuation-ring]]. A **discrete valuation ring** (DVR) is a subring $V\subseteq K$ of the form $V=V_v$ for some discrete valuation $v$ on $K$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is $$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$ The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying $$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$ A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with the analogous right-handed axioms.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is $$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$ The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left $A$-module. - Its **radical** is $$ \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M, $$ equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]]. - Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$, where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set.

after.quote:
Let $K$ be a field and let $v$ be a discrete valuation on $K$
([[def-discrete-valuation]]). Its **valuation ring** is
$$ V_v:=\{x\in K:v(x)\ge 0\}. $$
This is a valuation ring in the sense of [[def-valuation-ring]].

A **discrete valuation ring** (DVR) is a subring $V\subseteq K$ of the form
$V=V_v$ for some discrete valuation $v$ on $K$. Because $v$ is surjective,
there is an element of value $1$, so $V$ has a nonunit and is therefore not a
field.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$) with
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

before.claim: Smith reduction of the form. View $b$ as the $O$-linear map $\varphi\colon M\to M^*$, $\varphi(x)=b(x,-)$, with matrix $G$ in chosen bases by [F2]; nondegeneracy over $\operatorname{Frac}(O)$ gives $\det G\ne0$, so $\varphi$ has full rank. Choose a matrix entry of $\varphi$ of least valuation $\nu_\pi$ and move it to position $(1,1)$ by permuting the bases, then multiply its row by a unit of $O$ to make it $\pi^{a_1}$; every entry of the matrix is divisible by $\pi^{a_1}$ by minimality. Subtracting suitable $O$-multiples of the first row from the other rows and of the first column from the other columns (all coefficients in $O$, all operations unimodular by [F1]) kills the first row and column outside position $(1,1)$, leaving a smaller matrix over $O$. Iterating over the remaining rows and columns produces bases $u_1,\dots,u_n$ of $M$ and $v_1,\dots,v_n$ of $M^*$ with $\varphi(u_j)=\pi^{a_j}v_j$ and $0\le a_1\le\dots\le a_n$. [F1, F2, construct]

Reduction of the radical. For $\bar x\in M_F$ one has $b_F(\bar x,M_F)=0$ if and only if $b(x,M)\subseteq\pi O$, i.e. $x\in M(1)$; hence $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)=(M(1)+\pi M)/\pi M=M_F^1$ by [F3], the containment $\pi M\subseteq M(1)$ being immediate from $b(\pi x,M)\subseteq\pi O$. [F3, algebra]

Submodule stability. Let $a\in A$ and $x\in M(s)$; by the hypothesis $b(ax,y)=b(x,a^*y)\in\pi^sO$ for every $y\in M$, since $a^*y\in M$. Hence $ax\in M(s)$ and $M(s)$ is an $A$-submodule; consequently $M_F^s=(M(s)+\pi M)/\pi M$ is an $A$-submodule of $M_F$, the $\pi M$-cosets of $M(s)$ being stable because $\pi M$ is stable. [F3, algebra]

The cellular standard module. Assume $M_F$ is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, and let $N\subseteq M_F$ be a proper submodule. If some $w\in N$ lies outside $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, choose a label $v$ with $b_F(v,w)\ne0$; by the rank-one action [F4] every basis vector $u$ equals $b_F(v,w)^{-1}$ times the image of $w$ under the cell element of the pair $(u,v)$, so $u\in N$ for every basis label $u$ and $N=M_F$, a contradiction. Thus every proper submodule is contained in $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, which is proper because the form is nonzero, and the same rank-one argument shows that the quotient $M_F/\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is simple (it has no nonzero proper submodule). Hence $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is the unique maximal submodule of $M_F$, i.e. its module radical by [F3]. [F3, F4, algebra]

The filtration in the Smith bases. In the bases of step 1.1 one computes for $s\ge0$ that $b(u_j,M)=\pi^{a_j}O$, so $M(s)=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\pi^{\max(0,s-a_j)}Ou_j,\qquad \dim_FM_F^s=\#\{j:a_j\ge s\}.$ In particular $M(0)=M$, so $M_F^0=M/\pi M$; the filtration terminates because $M(s)=0$ for $s>\max_ja_j$; and each $M_F^s$ is a subspace of the finite-dimensional $F$-space $M_F$. [step 1.1, algebra]

The Gram valuation identity. By the matrix form of step 1.1, the determinant of $G$ equals $\det(\pi^{a_j}\delta_{jk})$ times a unit, since both change-of-basis matrices are invertible over $O$; hence, using additivity of $\nu_\pi$ by [F1], $\nu_\pi(\det G)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j =\sum_{s>0}\#\{j:a_j\ge s\} =\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s,$ the middle equality counting each $a_j$ as the number of positive integers $s\le a_j$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Conclusion. Steps 1.2–1.4 and 2.1–3.1 establish all four assertions of the Statement: the identification of $M_F^0$ and $M_F^1=\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, the termination together with the exact identity $\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G)$, the submodule stability under an anti-involution action, and the equality of $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ with the module radical in the cellular standard case. The Smith reduction of step 1.1 is valid over any discrete valuation ring, including residue characteristic $2$, because it uses independent domain and codomain bases and no symmetric diagonalization. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

after.claim: The rank-zero case. If $n=0$, then $M=0$ and $M^*=0$, the pairing is generically nondegenerate on the zero space, and $M(s)=M_F^s=0$ for every $s$. The empty Gram determinant is defined here by the empty Leibniz product to be $1$, whose valuation is $0$; the empty sum of elementary-divisor exponents is $0$. Thus the Gram valuation identity is $0=0$, the radical and stability assertions hold, and the conditional nonzero-cellular-form assertion has no rank-zero instance. For the remaining steps assume $n\ge1$.

Smith reduction of the form. View $b$ as the $O$-linear map $\varphi\colon M\to M^*$, $\varphi(x)=b(x,-)$, with matrix $G^{\mathsf T}$ in column coordinates by [F2]; nondegeneracy over $\operatorname{Frac}(O)$ gives $\det G\ne0$, so $\varphi$ has full rank. Choose a nonzero matrix entry of $\varphi$ of least valuation $\nu_\pi$ and move it to position $(1,1)$ by permuting the bases, then multiply its row by a unit of $O$ to make it $\pi^{a_1}$; every entry of the matrix is divisible by $\pi^{a_1}$ by minimality (including zero entries). Subtracting suitable $O$-multiples of the first row from the other rows and of the first column from the other columns (all coefficients in $O$, all operations unimodular by [F1]) kills the first row and column outside position $(1,1)$, leaving a smaller matrix over $O$. Iterating over the remaining rows and columns produces bases $u_1,\dots,u_n$ of $M$ and $v_1,\dots,v_n$ of $M^*$ with $\varphi(u_j)=\pi^{a_j}v_j$ and $0\le a_1\le\dots\le a_n$.

Reduction of the radical. For $\bar x\in M_F$ one has $b_F(\bar x,M_F)=0$ if and only if $b(x,M)\subseteq\pi O$, i.e. $x\in M(1)$; hence $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)=(M(1)+\pi M)/\pi M=M_F^1$ by [F3], the containment $\pi M\subseteq M(1)$ being immediate from $b(\pi x,M)\subseteq\pi O$.

Submodule stability. Let $a\in A$ and $x\in M(s)$; by the hypothesis $b(ax,y)=b(x,a^*y)\in\pi^sO$ for every $y\in M$, since $a^*y\in M$. Hence $ax\in M(s)$ and $M(s)$ is an $A$-submodule; consequently $M_F^s=(M(s)+\pi M)/\pi M$ is an $A$-submodule of $M_F$, the $\pi M$-cosets of $M(s)$ being stable because $\pi M$ is stable.

The cellular standard module. Assume $M_F$ is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, and let $N\subseteq M_F$ be a proper submodule. If some $w\in N$ lies outside $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, choose a label $v$ with $b_F(v,w)\ne0$; by the rank-one action [F4] every basis vector $u$ equals $b_F(v,w)^{-1}$ times the image of $w$ under the cell element of the pair $(u,v)$, so $u\in N$ for every basis label $u$ and $N=M_F$, a contradiction. Thus every proper submodule is contained in $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, which is proper because the form is nonzero, and the same rank-one argument shows that the quotient $M_F/\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is simple (it has no nonzero proper submodule). Hence $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is the unique maximal submodule of $M_F$, i.e. its module radical by [F3].

The filtration in the Smith bases. In the bases of step 1.2 one computes for $s\ge0$ that $b(u_j,M)=\pi^{a_j}O$, so $M(s)=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\pi^{\max(0,s-a_j)}Ou_j,\qquad \dim_FM_F^s=\#\{j:a_j\ge s\}.$ In particular $M(0)=M$, so $M_F^0=M/\pi M$; the reduced filtration terminates because every summand of $M(s)$ is contained in $\pi M$ for $s>\max_ja_j$, so $M_F^s=0$; and each $M_F^s$ is a subspace of the finite-dimensional $F$-space $M_F$.

The Gram valuation identity. By the matrix form of step 1.2, the determinant of $G$ equals that of $G^{\mathsf T}$ and hence $\det(\pi^{a_j}\delta_{jk})$ times a unit, since both change-of-basis matrices are invertible over $O$; hence, using additivity of $\nu_\pi$ by [F1], $\nu_\pi(\det G)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j =\sum_{s>0}\#\{j:a_j\ge s\} =\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s,$ the middle equality counting each $a_j$ as the number of positive integers $s\le a_j$.

Conclusion. The rank-zero argument of step 1.1 and steps 1.3–1.5 and 2.1–3.1 establish all four assertions of the Statement: the identification of $M_F^0$ and $M_F^1=\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, the termination together with the exact identity $\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G)$, the submodule stability under an anti-involution action, and the equality of $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ with the module radical in the cellular standard case. The Smith reduction of step 1.2 is valid over any discrete valuation ring, including residue characteristic $2$, because it uses independent domain and codomain bases and no symmetric diagonalization.

before.quote: Let $O$ be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$ and residue field $F=O/\pi O$ ([[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and let $\nu_\pi$ denote its valuation. Let $M$ be a finite free $O$-module with an $O$-valued bilinear pairing $b$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]) whose scalar extension to $\operatorname{Frac}(O)$ is nondegenerate.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying $$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$ A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with the analogous right-handed axioms.

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category ([[def-abelian-category]]). Its set of isomorphism classes is denoted $\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)$. The **Grothendieck group** of $\mathcal C$ is $$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle.

after.quote:
Let $O$ be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$ and residue field
$F=O/\pi O$ ([[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and let $\nu_\pi$ denote its
valuation. Let $M$ be a finite free $O$-module with an $O$-valued bilinear
pairing $b$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]) whose scalar extension to
$\operatorname{Frac}(O)$ is nondegenerate. For $s\ge0$ put
$$M(s):=\{x\in M:b(x,M)\subseteq\pi^sO\},\qquad M_F^s:=(M(s)+\pi M)/\pi M .$$
Then:

1. $M_F^0=M/\pi M$ and $M_F^1=\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, where $b_F$ is the
   reduced pairing on $M_F$;
2. the filtration terminates ($M_F^s=0$ for all sufficiently large $s$), and
   for any Gram matrix $G$ of $b$ one has the exact identity
   $$\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G);$$
3. if an $O$-algebra $A$ acts on $M$ with an anti-involution $*$ satisfying
   $b(ax,y)=b(x,a^*y)$ for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in M$, then every $M(s)$, and
   hence every $M_F^s$, is an $A$-submodule;
4. if $M_F$ is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form
   ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]), then
   $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is its unique maximal submodule and therefore
   coincides with its module radical
   ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]).

The Smith reduction used in the proof works over $O$ without any
characteristic restriction, in particular in characteristic $2$; it uses
independent bases of $M$ and of $M^*=\operatorname{Hom}_O(M,O)$, never a
diagonalization of a symmetric form.

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category
([[def-abelian-category]]). Its set of isomorphism classes is denoted
$\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)$. The **Grothendieck group** of $\mathcal C$ is

$$ G_0(\mathcal C):=\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]\big/\langle e_Y-e_X-e_Z:\ 0\to X\to Y\to Z\to 0\text{ is short exact in }\mathcal C\rangle. $$

where $\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal C)]$ is the free abelian group on
that set ([[def-free-abelian-group]]) and $[X]$ denotes the image of the
generator for the isomorphism class of $X$. Thus the defining relation is
$[Y]=[X]+[Z]$ for every short exact sequence
([[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]]).
This is the short-exact-sequence group, distinguished below from split
Grothendieck groups of projectives. No free abelian group on the possibly
class-sized collection of all objects is formed. The sequence
$0\to0\to0\to0$ in particular gives $[0]=0$.

u^*=e_
u$ and orthogonality, so $M_
u$ and $M_ho$ are orthogonal for $b$. If $x\in M_
u$ is orthogonal to $M_
u$, then it is orthogonal to every $M_ho$ (orthogonality) and hence to $M$, so $x=0$ by generic nondegeneracy of $b$; thus the restriction of $b$ to $M_

Exactness and the character map. The functor $N\mapsto e_
u N$ on $A$-modules is exact: a morphism commutes with $e_
u$, so its kernel on $e_
u N$ is $e_
u$ times its kernel on $N$; if $y=e_

Injectivity of the weight character. Write a class in $K_0$ as $\sum_\mu a_\mu[\Delta(\mu)]$ with $a_\mu\in\mathbb Z$. Its coordinates on the partition weights are the row vector $a=(a_\mu)$ multiplied by the matrix $K=(K_{\mu
u})$, $K_{\mu
u}=\dim e_

On the square unitriangular submatrix indexed by the partition weights, $K$ is invertible over $\mathbb Z$ by finite triangular elimination (all diagonal entries are $1$); if $\operatorname{ch}(a)=0$, then the coordinates on that submatrix vanish and the triangular system forces $a_\mu=0$ for every $\mu$. Hence $\operatorname{ch}$ is injective.

The Jantzen filtration decomposes. For each $s$ the orthogonality of the summands gives $M(s)= igoplus_
u M_
u(s)$ with $M_
u(s)=\{x\in M_
u:b(x,M_
u)\subseteq\pi^sO\}$, because the components of $x$ in the other summands pair trivially; consequently $M_F^s= igoplus_

u=0$, each $e_

u_\pi(\det G_
u)$.

Conclusion. By step 2.1, the multiplicities appearing in a Jantzen class equality are exactly the weight Gram valuations $\nu_\pi(\det G_\nu)$; by step 1.4 the weight character detects class equalities, so a class equality involving Jantzen pieces holds if and only if the corresponding equalities of weight Gram valuations hold. No Schur functor, residue-sequence character, rationalization or semisimple Hecke Grothendieck group is used anywhere.

before.quote: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge1$, and let $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$ be units of $R$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]).

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations $(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with $T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): 1.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation $$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$ where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition $(i\ i+1)$.

after.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge1$, and let $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$
be units of $R$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). The **arbitrary-level
cyclotomic Hecke algebra** $H_n=H_n(R;z;U_1,\dots,U_\ell)$ is the $R$-algebra
presented by invertible commuting elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ subject to the relations
$$(T_i-z)(T_i+1)=0,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$
$$T_iX_iT_i=zX_{i+1},\qquad X_jT_i=T_iX_j\quad(j\notin\{i,i+1\}),\qquad \prod_{a=1}^{\ell}(X_1-U_a)=0 .$$
For $n=0$ set $H_0=R$. The **grading variable** of this page is $v$, not the
unit $z$: the two are identified only where a statement says so explicitly.

**Multipartitions and Murphy data.** An $\ell$-**multipartition** of $n$ is an
ordered tuple $\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(\ell)})$ of partitions
with $\sum_{b}|\lambda^{(b)}|=n$ ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).
Multipartitions are partially ordered by dominance, $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ meaning
that $\sum_{b\le k}|\lambda^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\lambda^{(k)}_j\ge
\sum_{b\le k}|\mu^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\mu^{(k)}_j$ for all $k,m$. Fill the
diagram $t^\lambda$ with $1,\dots,n$ in component order, then row order, then
column order. Put $a_k:=\sum_{b<k}|\lambda^{(b)}|$,
$u_\lambda:=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell}\prod_{j\le a_k}(X_j-U_k)$,
$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, and $m_\lambda:=x_\lambda u_\lambda$,
where $S_\lambda$ is the row subgroup: the subgroup of $S_n$ stabilizing the
rows of $t^\lambda$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $M_\lambda:=m_\lambda H_n$ for
the right $H_n$-submodule generated by $m_\lambda$
([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). The **presentation involution** $*$ of $H_n$
fixes every $X_j$ and every $T_i$ and reverses products. For standard
tableaux $s,t$ of shape $\lambda$ put $m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$,
where $d(s)$ is the permutation determined by $t^\lambda d(s)=s$.
Denote by $H^{>\lambda}$ the span of the higher Murphy shapes once their
basis and cell law is established by
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]], and by
$S_\lambda$ the right cell (**Specht**) module with basis $m_t$ and the
action given by that cell law; its cellular form defines
$D_\lambda:=S_\lambda/\operatorname{rad}S_\lambda$, which may vanish.

**Types.** The types used below are **exactly** all $\ell$-multipartitions of
$n$, including tuples with empty components — not all multicompositions. A
**semistandard tableau** $S$ has entries the labels $(i,k)$ (row $i$ in
component $k$) ordered by component first and then by row, weakly increasing
along rows, strictly increasing down columns, and a label of component $a$
may occur only in physical component $b\le a$
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]); the **type** of $S$ is the
multipartition counting each label with the multiplicity of the corresponding
row. For standard $s$ let $\mu(s)$ be the tableau obtained from $s$ by
replacing each entry by its row-and-component in $t^{\mu}$. Put
$$m_{(S,t)}:=\sum_{s:\,\mu(s)=S}m_{st},\qquad m_{(S,T)}:=\sum_{s,t:\,\mu(s)=S,\ \nu(t)=T}m_{st}.$$
Let
$$M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda\ \text{multipartition of}\ n}M_\lambda,\qquad C_n:=\operatorname{End}_{H_n}(M),$$
with ordinary composition ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]). For
$S,T$ of shape $\lambda$ and types $\mu,\nu$, the map $\varphi_{ST}$ — once
justified by [[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] —
sends $m_\alpha h$ to $\delta_{\alpha,\nu}m_{(S,T)}h$. Its right cell module
$\Delta_\lambda$ has basis $v_T$ over the semistandard $T$ of multipartition
types, with contravariant cell form and quotient $L_\lambda$. Let $T^\lambda$
be the unique tableau of shape and type $\lambda$, and let $e_\lambda$ be the
identity projection onto $M_\lambda$. Put $\omega:=(\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing,(1^n))$
and $e:=e_\omega$; then $m_\omega=1$, so $M_\omega=H_n$, and $H_n$ is an
actual direct summand of $M$. The weight projections used by the Jantzen
theory below are the $e_\nu$ with $\nu$ a multipartition. Write
$K_{(\lambda,\nu)}:=\#\operatorname{SStd}_\nu(\lambda)$ for the number of
semistandard tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and type $\nu$.

**Boundary of the definition.** All asserted module, form and map laws are
discharged by the linked local suppliers
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]],
[[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] and
[[thm-cyclotomic-schur-standards-and-schur-functor-control-block-linkage]];
the definition itself claims no proof of them and no primitive
residue-content classification. No choice principle is used: only finite
bases, finite subgroup and coset decompositions, finite filtrations and
explicit polynomial identities occur.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation

$$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition
$(i\ i+1)$. For
$n=0,1$, the trivial group has the empty presentation.

before.claim: Spanning by ordered monomials. The Bernstein relation, read as $T_iX_i=X_{i+1}T_i-(z-1)X_{i+1}$ and $X_iT_i=T_iX_{i+1}-(z-1)X_{i+1}$ (both consequences of $T_iX_iT_i=zX_{i+1}$ and [F2]), together with the distant commutation $T_iX_j=X_jT_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$, moves every $X$-symbol in a word past the $T$-symbols at the cost of terms with the same number of $X$-symbols and a strictly smaller number of $(T,X)$-inversions; iterating rewrites any element as an $R$-combination of the $X^aT_w$. The subalgebra generated by the $T_i$ is spanned by the $T_w$ by [F2], and the $X$'s commute, so the family $X^aT_w$, $a\in\mathbb Z^n$, $w\in S_n$, spans $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$; applying the presentation anti-involution (which fixes the $X_i$ and $T_i$ and reverses products) gives the same spanning statement for the family $T_wX^a$. [F1, F2, algebra]

The rational representation. Let $K$ be the fraction field of the commutative Laurent polynomial ring $R[X_1^{\pm1},\dots,X_n^{\pm1}]$, considered as the field of rational functions in the commuting variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ over the fraction field of $R$; form the crossed product algebra $K\rtimes S_n$ with $K$-basis the group elements and multiplication $f\sigma\cdot g\tau=f\,\sigma(g)\,\sigma\tau$. Put $c_{ij}:=\frac{(z-1)X_j}{X_j-X_i},\qquad d_{ij}:=\frac{X_j-zX_i}{X_j-X_i}=-\frac{X_j}{X_j-X_i}c_{ij}+1,\qquad T_i:=c_{i,i+1}+d_{i,i+1}s_i .$ Substituting these rational functions and clearing the nonzero denominators $X_j-X_i$, the following identities are checked directly in the polynomial ring: $c_{ij}+c_{ji}=z-1$; $d_{ij}d_{ji}=z+(z-1)c_{ij}-c_{ij}^2$; and, for three distinct indices, $c_{ij}c_{jk}=c_{ik}(c_{ij}+c_{jk}-(z-1))$. They imply that the $T_i$ satisfy the quadratic relation $(T_i-z)(T_i+1)=0$ and the braid relation, while distant generators involve disjoint variable pairs and commute; the $T_i$ also satisfy the Bernstein relations with the multiplication operators $X_j$ by direct substitution. Consequently the assignment of [F1] defines an $R$-algebra homomorphism from the localization $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}[(X_i-X_j)^{-1}]$ to $K\rtimes S_n$. [F1, algebra]

Independence of the ordered monomials. Fix a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ and expand $T_w=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_k}$ in the $K$-basis of $K\rtimes S_n$; the term in which the factor $d_{i_t,i_t+1}s_{i_t}$ is chosen from every $T_{i_t}$ contributes the scalar $\prod_td_{i_t,i_t+1}\ne0$ times the permutation $s_w$, while every other term contains the product of a proper subword of $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, hence a permutation of strictly smaller length by [F3]. So the coefficient of $s_w$ in $T_w$ is a nonzero product of $d$-functions and all other occurring permutations are proper Bruhat subwords. To see that the resulting triangular system forces independence, apply a putative $K\rtimes S_n$ dependence $\sum_{a,w}\lambda_{a,w}X^aT_w=0$ to the element $f:=\sum_{j=1}^njX_j$: the crossed-product identity $X^aT_w(f)$ expands as a rational function $X^a\,\bigl(T_w(f)\bigr)$ plus terms of strictly lower permutation length, and the leading contributions $X^a\,w(f)$, indexed by distinct $a$ and distinct $w$, are pairwise distinct Laurent monomials times $w(f)$; a maximal leading monomial in a dependence would have to cancel against several equal monomials, and within a fixed $(a,w)$ the coefficient of the top monomial of $X^aw(f)$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of the triangular coefficient of $T_w$, which is nonzero. Hence all $\lambda_{a,w}=0$ and the family $X^aT_w$ is $K$-independent; the same argument applied after the anti-involution gives the independence of $T_wX^a$. Since $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ is the base change of its localization along the injective map of domains, and the change-of-basis from $X^aT_w$ to the spanning set is triangular with unit diagonal over $R$, the family is an $R$-basis, and it stays a basis after any base change in which $z$ remains a unit. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

The intertwiners after localizing at the differences. In the localized algebra set $\Phi_i:=T_i-c_{i,i+1}$. For $f$ a (localized) Laurent polynomial, the Bernstein relations of [F1] give $T_if=s_i(f)T_i+\gamma_i(f),\qquad \Phi_if=T_if-c_{i,i+1}f=s_i(f)T_i+\gamma_i(f)-c_{i,i+1}f$ with a correction $\gamma_i(f)$ supported on terms with no $s_i$; substituting $c_{i,i+1}=\frac{(z-1)X_{i+1}}{X_{i+1}-X_i}$ and clearing denominators shows $s_i(f)\Phi_i=s_i(f)T_i-s_i(f)c_{i,i+1}$ agrees with the previous display, so $\Phi_if=s_i(f)\Phi_i .$ Only the three nonzero differences occurring in $c_{i,i+1}$, $s_i(c_{i,i+1})$ and $s_i(f)$ are inverted; no $U_a-U_b$, quantum factorial or Gram determinant is inverted. [F1, algebra]

Injectivity of left multiplication and the right basis. Every element of $P:=R[X_1^{\pm1},\dots,X_n^{\pm1}]$ is a nonzero-divisor in $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$: writing the basis expansion $h=\sum_wX^{a(w)}T_w$ with $X^{a(w)}\in P$ and multiplying on the left by $0\ne f\in P$ gives $\sum_w(fX^{a(w)})T_w$, and the first basis assertion forces $fX^{a(w)}=0$ for every $w$, i.e. $X^{a(w)}=0$, since $P$ is a domain and the $X_i$ are units. Hence left multiplication by any nonzero Laurent polynomial is injective, and the same argument with the right basis gives the analogous statement for right multiplication. [step 1.1, step 1.3, algebra]

Subword expansion and the crossed-product embedding. Expanding each $T_{i_t}$ in a reduced word as $\Phi_{i_t}+c_{i_t,i_{t+1}}$ and repeatedly using step 1.4, the product $T_wf$ becomes a sum of terms $v(f)\cdot\kappa_v$ in which $v$ runs through the subwords of $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ (with the empty subword contributing the identity permutation) and each coefficient $\kappa_v$ is a sum of products of the $c$'s and $d$'s, so its denominator is a product of differences $X_i-X_j$ with $i\ne j$. By [F3] each such $v$ is Bruhat-below $w$. Hence the localization map of step 1.2 is defined on $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}[(X_i-X_j)^{-1}]$ and its kernel is zero on the basis expansion of every element, i.e. the map embeds the localized algebra into $K\rtimes S_n$, and the intertwining relation of step 1.4 holds throughout the image. [F3, step 1.2, step 1.4, algebra]

Conclusion. Steps 1.1 and 1.3 show that $X^aT_w$ and $T_wX^a$ ($a\in\mathbb Z^n$, $w\in S_n$) are both $R$-bases of $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$, over the universal Laurent parameter ring and after any base change in which $z$ is a unit; step 2.1 gives injectivity of left multiplication by a nonzero Laurent polynomial; steps 1.4 and 2.2 give the embedding into the rational crossed product and the relation $\Phi_if=s_i(f)\Phi_i$. No cyclotomic basis, Brundan–Kleshchev theorem, trace form or primitive-content assertion is used anywhere in the argument. [step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

after.claim: Ordered spanning without localization. For every $f\in P$ the presentation relations give $T_if=s_i(f)T_i+c_{i,i+1}(f-s_i(f))$, where $c_{i,i+1}=(z-1)X_{i+1}/(X_{i+1}-X_i)$. The correction is in $P$: $f-s_i(f)$ is divisible by $X_{i+1}-X_i$, first for ordinary monomials by the difference-of-powers identity, and then for Laurent monomials after multiplying by a symmetric Laurent monomial unit. For $f=X_i$ this is the Bernstein relation, for $f=X_{i+1}$ it is its conjugate using the quadratic relation, and the general formula follows by addition and the product rule $f g-s_i(f g)=(f-s_i(f))g+s_i(f)(g-s_i(g))$, including inverse generators by applying that rule to $f f^{-1}=1$. Moving a polynomial across a $T$ reduces the number of misplaced polynomial factors, and correction terms reduce the number of $T$ factors; the finite Hecke relations then span the remaining words by $T_w$. Thus $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ is spanned over $P$ by the $T_w$, and the presentation anti-involution fixing $X_i,T_i$ gives right ordered spanning too.

A representation of the unlocalized presentation. Form $K\rtimes S_n$ with multiplication $(f\sigma)(g\tau)=f\sigma(g)\sigma\tau$. For distinct indices set $c_{ij}=(z-1)X_j/(X_j-X_i)$ and $d_{ij}=(X_j-zX_i)/(X_j-X_i)=z-c_{ij}$, and assign $T_i\mapsto c_{i,i+1}+d_{i,i+1}s_i$, $X_j\mapsto X_j$. The rational identities $c_{ij}+c_{ji}=z-1$ and $d_{ij}d_{ji}=z+(z-1)c_{ij}-c_{ij}^2$ give the quadratic relation. For three distinct indices, expansion of the two braid products in their six permutation coefficients agrees: the longest coefficients are $d_{ij}d_{ik}d_{jk}$ in either order; the two length-two coefficients agree by commuting scalar factors; the length-one and identity coefficients agree using $c_{ij}c_{jk}=c_{ik}(c_{ij}+c_{jk}-(z-1))$ together with the preceding quadratic identities. These identities follow by multiplying by the common product of the differences and expanding the polynomial numerators. Distant relations follow from disjoint variable pairs. Finally $T_if-s_i(f)T_i=c_{i,i+1}(f-s_i(f))$, so the Bernstein and mixed relations hold. All denominators here are nonzero polynomials in independent variables in the domain $P$. This defines a homomorphism from the unlocalized presented algebra to $K\rtimes S_n$.

Independence over the base ring. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, the coefficient of the group element $w$ in the image of $T_w$ is
$$D_w=d_{i_1,i_1+1}\,s_{i_1}(d_{i_2,i_2+1})\cdots(s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_{k-1}})(d_{i_k,i_k+1})\ne0.$$
Every factor is a nonzero rational function; every other term uses a proper subword and therefore represents a permutation of length less than $k$ by [F3]. In a finite relation $\sum_w f_wT_w=0$ with $f_w\in P$, select a label $w$ of maximal length with $f_w\ne0$. Its group-element coefficient is $f_wD_w$ and receives no contribution from any other label of that maximal length or from shorter labels, so it is nonzero in $K$, a contradiction. Hence the $T_w$ are $P$-linearly independent and the representation is injective. Since the Laurent monomials $X^a$ are an $R$-basis of $P$, this proves that $X^aT_w$ are an $R$-basis; the anti-involution proves the right basis. Tensoring this free basis with any commutative $R$-algebra preserves it, and tensoring the generators-and-relations presentation gives exactly the same affine presentation over that algebra. As the unused $U$ parameters do not enter the relations, any commutative coefficient ring with unit $z$ is obtained by sending every $U_a$ to $1$. Thus the asserted arbitrary base change is valid, without inverting differences in the base-changed algebra.

Localization and intertwiners. Let $S$ be the multiplicative set generated by all $X_i-X_j$ with $i\ne j$. It is invariant under $S_n$. The mixed formula of step 1.1 extends to $S^{-1}P$ by the same product rule and by solving the formula for inverses of elements of $S$; the correction remains in $S^{-1}P$. Consequently adjoining these inverses gives the algebra with free left coefficient module $\bigoplus_w(S^{-1}P)T_w$ and the same multiplication rules. This realizes the localization: the inverse formulas make it universal among homomorphisms inverting $S$, and its injective representation in $K\rtimes S_n$ follows from the identical maximal-length argument of step 1.3. In it put $\Phi_i=T_i-c_{i,i+1}$; the mixed formula gives $\Phi_if=s_i(f)\Phi_i$ for all $f\in S^{-1}P$. Products $\Phi_w$ along reduced words have unitriangular expansions in the $T_v$, because selecting every $T$ gives $T_w$ and selecting any scalar correction leaves strictly shorter words; thus they too form a basis over $S^{-1}P$. No parameter difference $U_a-U_b$, quantum factorial or Gram determinant is inverted.

Polynomial multiplication is injective over the universal domain. If $0\ne f\in P$ and $h=\sum_w f_wT_w$, then $fh=0$ gives $ff_w=0$ for each $w$ by step 1.3. Since $P$ is a domain, every $f_w=0$, so $h=0$. The right-basis argument gives the analogous right multiplication result. This injectivity assertion is over the universal domain, as in Statement (2), and does not assert injectivity of nonzero zero divisors after arbitrary base change.

Subword support in the localization. Expanding a reduced product $T_w=\prod_t(\Phi_{i_t}+c_{i_t,i_t+1})$ and moving coefficients left using step 2.1 gives terms supported on products of subwords of the reduced word. Every coefficient is a sum of products of permuted $c$ functions and hence has only variable-difference denominators. Equivalently, in the crossed product $\Phi_i=d_{i,i+1}s_i$, so moving a localized polynomial $f$ through such a term replaces it by the corresponding subword permutation applied to $f$. This proves the subword expansion used by consumers and the asserted intertwining throughout the embedded localization.

Conclusion. Step 1.3 proves both ordered bases over $R$ and after arbitrary base change with unit $z$; step 2.2 proves the universal-domain injectivity; and steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the localized embedding and intertwining identity. For $n=0$ there are no polynomial or Hecke generators, $S_0$ consists of the identity, the lone ordered monomial is $1$, and $H_0^{\mathrm{aff}}=R$; all localization and intertwining clauses are then vacuous. No cyclotomic basis, trace form, primitive-content assertion or Brundan–Kleshchev result is used.
